stem: Which of the following must be true?
stimulus:
A hydrologist selected 200 wells at random from the 5,000 private wells in a county and tested each one. Of the wells tested, 18% had nitrate levels above the safe drinking-water limit.

I. The sample result of 18% is an estimate of the percent of all 5,000 wells in the county with nitrate levels above the limit.
II. Exactly 18% of all 5,000 wells in the county have nitrate levels above the limit.
explanation: The 200 wells were chosen at random from the county's 5,000 wells, so the sample percent is a reasonable estimate of the percent for all 5,000 wells. That makes statement I true. A sample statistic is never guaranteed to equal the population value exactly, so statement II doesn't have to be true.

B.why: You treated the sample percent as the exact percent for every well in the county. Random selection makes 18% a reasonable estimate, not a guaranteed value.

C.why: You saw correctly that statement I is true, but you also accepted statement II. The sample only estimates the county-wide percent and can't fix it at exactly 18%.

D.why: You rejected every statement, including the hedged one. Statement I only says the sample result estimates the population value, and for a random sample that is true.

stem: Which of the following must be true?
stimulus: A mapping agency checked 400 intersections selected at random from its digital street map of a city. For each intersection, it measured how far the mapped location was from the true location. The mean positional error of the 400 intersections was 3.2 meters.
choices: The mean positional error of all intersections on the city map is 3.2 meters.
The value 3.2 meters is an estimate of the mean positional error for all intersections on the city map.
Each of the 400 intersections that were checked has a positional error of 3.2 meters.
The mean positional error of all intersections on a nearby city's map is 3.2 meters.
explanation: The intersections were selected at random from this city's map, so the sample mean of 3.2 meters estimates the mean error for all intersections on that map. Nothing guarantees that the population mean is exactly 3.2 meters.

A.why: You assumed the sample mean equals the population mean exactly because the sample was random. Random selection makes 3.2 meters a reasonable estimate. It doesn't make it exact.

C.why: You treated a mean as if it were every individual value. A mean of 3.2 meters can come from errors that are bigger and smaller than 3.2 meters.

D.why: You applied the result to a population that was never sampled. Only this city's intersections were checked, so the result says nothing certain about another city's map.

stem: Which of the following must be true?
stimulus:
A research farm is divided into 1,200 wheat plots. An agronomist selected 60 of the plots at random and measured their harvests. The mean yield of the 60 plots was 4.5 tons per hectare.

I. The mean yield of 4.5 tons per hectare is an estimate of the mean yield of all 1,200 plots.
II. The mean yield of all 1,200 plots is exactly 4.5 tons per hectare.
explanation: The 60 plots were a random sample of the farm's 1,200 plots, so their mean yield estimates the mean yield of all 1,200 plots. That makes statement I true. The estimate isn't guaranteed to be exact, so statement II doesn't have to be true.

B.why: You decided the farm-wide mean must match the sample mean exactly. A random sample gives a reasonable estimate of the population mean, not its exact value.

C.why: You accepted statement I correctly but also accepted statement II. The word 'exactly' is a claim the sample can't support.

D.why: You rejected statement I even though it only says the sample mean is an estimate. For a random sample of the plots, that is true.

stem: Which of the following must be true?
stimulus: A city planning office surveyed 500 residents selected at random from the city. Of those surveyed, 62% said they support adding protected bike lanes on the city's main avenue.
choices: Exactly 62% of all residents of the city support the protected bike lanes.
A second random sample of 500 city residents would show exactly 62% support.
Exactly 62% of residents of a neighboring suburb support the bike lanes.
None of the statements in choices A, B, and C must be true.
explanation: A random sample of 500 residents gives an estimate of the percent of all residents who support the bike lanes. It doesn't guarantee that the city-wide percent, a repeated sample, or a different town's percent is exactly 62%. None of the other statements must be true.

A.why: You took the sample percent as the exact city-wide percent. A random sample makes 62% a reasonable estimate, not a certainty.

B.why: You assumed that a new random sample would give an identical result. Results vary from one random sample to the next, so a second sample could easily come out a little higher or lower.

C.why: You extended the result to a population that wasn't sampled. Only city residents were surveyed, so the result tells you nothing certain about the suburb.

stem: Which of the following must be true?
stimulus:
Excavators recovered 2,000 pottery shards from a site. An archaeologist selected 80 of the shards at random and examined them. Of the 80 shards examined, 25% had painted decoration.

I. Exactly 25% of all 2,000 shards recovered from the site have painted decoration.
II. Exactly 20 of the 80 shards examined have painted decoration.
explanation: Statement II describes the sample itself: 25% of 80 is $0.25 \times 80 = 20$, so it must be true. Statement I claims the sample percent holds exactly for all 2,000 shards. The sample only estimates that percent, so statement I doesn't have to be true.

A.why: You treated the sample percent as the exact percent for every shard at the site. Random selection makes 25% a reasonable estimate, not an exact value.

C.why: You saw that statement II is true, but you also accepted statement I. A sample can't guarantee the exact percent for the whole collection of 2,000 shards.

D.why: You rejected statement II, but it is a fact about the sample, not a claim about the population. Since $0.25 \times 80 = 20$, it must be true.

stem: Which of the following must be true?
stimulus:
Researchers selected 250 adults at random from a city's registry of blood donors and tested their blood. Of the donors tested, 40% had antibodies to a particular virus.

I. Exactly 40% of all donors in the city's registry have antibodies to the virus.
II. Exactly 40% of all adults in the country have antibodies to the virus.
explanation: The sample estimates the percent of donors in the city's registry who have the antibodies, but it doesn't fix that percent at exactly 40%. Adults across the country weren't sampled at all. Neither statement must be true.

A.why: You assumed the registry-wide percent must equal the sample percent because the sample was random. Random selection gives a reasonable estimate, not an exact match.

B.why: You applied the result to a population the researchers never sampled. Only donors in one city's registry were tested, not all adults in the country.

C.why: You accepted both exact claims. The sample can't guarantee an exact value even for the registry it came from, and it says even less about the whole country.

stem: Which of the following must be true?
stimulus:
An astronomer selected 120 stars at random from a catalog of 9,000 stars and studied each one. Of the 120 stars studied, 15% were found to be members of binary star systems.

I. The percent of stars in the catalog that are members of binary systems can be estimated as 15%.
II. Exactly 18 of the 120 stars studied are members of binary systems.
explanation: The 120 stars were a random sample from the catalog, so 15% is a reasonable estimate for the whole catalog. That makes statement I true. Statement II describes the sample itself: $0.15 \times 120 = 18$, so it must also be true.

A.why: You accepted the estimate in statement I but missed that statement II is a fact about the sample. Since $0.15 \times 120 = 18$, statement II must also be true.

B.why: You accepted statement II but rejected statement I. Statement I doesn't claim the catalog is exactly 15% binary. It only calls 15% an estimate, which is true for a random sample.

D.why: You rejected both statements, but neither one claims an exact value for the population. One is a hedged estimate and the other is a count from the sample itself.

stem: Which of the following must be true?
stimulus: A marine biologist measured 50 sea turtles selected at random from the turtles that nest on a particular beach. The mean carapace (shell) length of the 50 turtles was 90 centimeters.
choices: The mean carapace length of all turtles nesting on the beach can be estimated as 90 centimeters.
The mean carapace length of all turtles nesting on the beach is exactly 90 centimeters.
A second random sample of 50 turtles from the beach would have a mean of exactly 90 centimeters.
The mean carapace length of turtles nesting on a different beach is exactly 90 centimeters.
explanation: The turtles were selected at random from those that nest on this beach, so the sample mean of 90 centimeters is a reasonable estimate of the mean for all turtles nesting there. It isn't guaranteed to be exact.

B.why: You took the sample mean to be the exact population mean. A random sample makes 90 centimeters a reasonable estimate, not a certainty.

C.why: You assumed that repeating the sampling would give the identical mean. Different random samples give different means, so a second sample would probably differ a little.

D.why: You extended the result to a population that wasn't sampled. Only turtles from this beach were measured, so the result guarantees nothing about turtles at another beach.
